newsitem.title: INDIA: India sets panel on intellectual property rights.
newsitem.headline: India sets panel on intellectual property rights.

text.p: The Indian government said on on Tuesday it had decided to set up a panel to evolve a national consensus on intellectual property rights.

The dispute settlement mechanism of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in a report has said that India has failed to comply with certain requirements of trade-related intellectual property rights (TRIPS), a government spokesman told reporters.

"Against this background it has been decided to set up an expert body to evolve a national consensus on a comprehensive approach to intellectual property regime and related issues to safeguard the national interest," the spokesman said.
The decision came after Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral met a panel of parliament deputies to discuss intellectual property rights and related issues.
India joined the WTO, which began operations in 1995, and pledged to bring its patents laws in line with new international requirements.

But the left-wing parties and the main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party last year in the upper house of parliament stalled a government-sponsored bill that would have added teeth to India's patents law by extending protection, currently covering only manufacturing processes, to products.
India was able to meet the WTO's patent requirements when it joined the organisation in 1995 by virtue of a presidential decree which temporarily protected products.
But the decree has expired, and legislation bringing India in line with its WTO commitment died before the upper house of parliament could approve it.
"The old bill is a closed chapter," a government official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters. "Prime Minister Gujral is trying to evolve a national consensus."
The United States and other Western nations have repeatedly urged India to protect intellectual property rights such as patents and copyrights.

"The battle has just begun and I am happy that we were able to arrive at a consensus over the setting up of the group," the Press Trust of India (PTI) quoted opposition socialist leader George Fernandes as saying.
India has a 10-year transitional period until 2005 in which to strengthen its intellectual property rights legislation in line with the WTO accord.
But during the interim period, India like other developing countries, is obliged under WTO rules to provide a means by which patent applications can be filed.
